mcqs.question: What is a Java package?

options.A: A compressed archive of .class files
options.B: A namespace container for organizing related classes, avoiding name collisions
options.C: A collection of Java programs stored on a disk
options.D: A way to import external libraries

mcqs.explanation: A package is a namespace that groups related classes and interfaces together. It helps avoid naming collisions (two classes with the same name in different packages), provides access control, and organizes code into logical modules.

mcqs.question: What is the Java statement used to declare which package a class belongs to?

options.A: import myPackage;
options.B: namespace myPackage;
options.C: package myPackage;
options.D: group myPackage;

mcqs.explanation: The 'package' statement declares the package a class belongs to. It must be the FIRST statement in a Java source file (before any import statements or class declaration). Example: 'package com.company.project;'

mcqs.question: What is the naming convention for Java packages?

options.A: PascalCase starting with uppercase
options.B: ALL_CAPS with underscores
options.C: Lowercase letters, often using reverse domain (com.company.project)
options.D: camelCase starting with lowercase letter

mcqs.explanation: Java package names are conventionally all lowercase. The standard convention is to use the reverse of your internet domain name: 'com.company.projectname'. This ensures globally unique package names and avoids naming conflicts between different organizations.

mcqs.question: What is a sub-package in Java?

options.A: A package with fewer than 5 classes
options.B: A package nested within another package using dot notation (e.g., java.util.concurrent)
options.C: A private package inaccessible from outside
options.D: A package that extends another package

mcqs.explanation: Sub-packages are packages nested within other packages. 'java.util.concurrent' is a sub-package of 'java.util'. They are created using hierarchical directory structures and allow further organization within large packages.

mcqs.question: What statement is used to make classes from another package available in the current file?

options.A: include java.util.Scanner;
options.B: use java.util.Scanner;
options.C: import java.util.Scanner;
options.D: require java.util.Scanner;

mcqs.explanation: The 'import' statement tells the Java compiler where to find classes from other packages. 'import java.util.Scanner;' allows using 'Scanner' directly instead of 'java.util.Scanner' everywhere in the file.

mcqs.question: What does 'import packageName.*;' do?

options.A: Imports all packages in the JDK
options.B: Imports all public classes and interfaces from the specified package
options.C: Creates a copy of all classes in the current package
options.D: Imports all methods from a specific class

mcqs.explanation: 'import packageName.*;' uses a wildcard to import all public classes and interfaces from the named package. For example, 'import java.util.*;' makes Scanner, ArrayList, HashMap, etc., all available without their full qualified names.

mcqs.question: Must a class intended to be used outside its package be declared public?

options.A: No — any class can be used from any package
options.B: Yes — only public classes are accessible from outside their package
options.C: Only if the class has public methods
options.D: Only if the class is in a named package

mcqs.explanation: A class must be declared public to be accessible from other packages. Default (no modifier) classes are package-private — visible only within their package. For a library class to be usable by other packages, it must be public.

mcqs.question: What is the primary advantage of using packages to avoid naming conflicts?

options.A: Packages rename classes automatically
options.B: Two different packages can have classes with the same name without conflict; fully qualified names distinguish them
options.C: Packages prevent compilation of duplicate class names
options.D: Packages encrypt class names

mcqs.explanation: Packages create separate namespaces. 'com.bank.Transaction' and 'com.retail.Transaction' are completely different classes despite the same simple name. The fully qualified name (package.ClassName) uniquely identifies each class globally.

mcqs.question: What are the two types of packages in Java?

options.A: System packages and application packages
options.B: Built-in API packages (from JDK) and user-defined packages
options.C: Compiled packages and source packages
options.D: Local packages and remote packages

mcqs.explanation: Java packages fall into two categories: 1) Built-in API packages provided by the JDK (java.lang, java.util, java.io, javax.swing, etc.), and 2) User-defined packages that developers create to organize their own code.

mcqs.question: What are the four key advantages of using packages?

options.A: Speed, memory, security, portability
options.B: Namespace collision avoidance, access control, reusability, maintainability
options.C: Compilation speed, runtime speed, debugging, testing
options.D: Documentation, versioning, distribution, installation

mcqs.explanation: The four advantages of packages as covered in the NPTEL lecture are: 1) Namespace collision avoidance (unique naming), 2) Access control (package-level visibility), 3) Reusability (package libraries), and 4) Maintainability (organized code structure).

mcqs.question: Where must the 'package' declaration appear in a Java source file?

options.A: After all import statements
options.B: Before everything else (must be the first non-comment statement)
options.C: After the class declaration
options.D: Anywhere in the file

mcqs.explanation: The 'package' statement must be the first non-comment, non-blank statement in a Java source file. It must come before any import statements and before the class declaration. Placing it elsewhere is a syntax error.

mcqs.question: How does Java's package structure relate to the directory structure on disk?

options.A: Packages and directories are unrelated
options.B: Package names map directly to directory paths: package com.bank.accounts corresponds to com/bank/accounts/
options.C: All packages reside in the root directory
options.D: Packages are stored in a database, not directories

mcqs.explanation: Java's package structure mirrors the filesystem: 'package com.bank.accounts' requires the .class file to be in 'com/bank/accounts/' directory relative to the classpath root. The JVM uses this directory structure to locate classes by their fully qualified names.

mcqs.question: What is a fully qualified class name?

options.A: A class name with at least 10 characters
options.B: The complete class identifier including package path: packageName.ClassName (e.g., java.util.Scanner)
options.C: A class name that includes the method names
options.D: A class name used only in import statements

mcqs.explanation: A fully qualified class name includes the complete package path: 'java.util.Scanner'. This uniquely identifies the class globally, distinguishing it from any other class named 'Scanner' in any other package. You can use fully qualified names without import statements.

mcqs.question: What happens if two imported packages have classes with the same name?

options.A: The compiler uses the first import
options.B: Compilation error due to ambiguity; use the fully qualified name to disambiguate
options.C: The JVM selects one at random
options.D: The second import overrides the first

mcqs.explanation: If 'import com.lib1.*;' and 'import com.lib2.*;' both have a class 'Manager', using 'Manager' in the code is ambiguous. The compiler reports an error. The solution is to use fully qualified names: 'com.lib1.Manager' or 'com.lib2.Manager' to explicitly specify which one.

mcqs.question: Can a class use another class in the same package without an import statement?

options.A: No — all classes need import statements
options.B: Yes — classes in the same package can use each other without importing
options.C: Only if both are public
options.D: Only if they are in the same source file

mcqs.explanation: Classes in the same package have automatic access to each other without import statements. Import is only needed when using classes from DIFFERENT packages. This is why java.lang doesn't need importing — it's automatically available.

mcqs.question: Is 'import java.lang.*;' necessary at the top of every Java file?

options.A: Yes — java.lang must always be explicitly imported
options.B: No — java.lang is automatically imported by the compiler for every file
options.C: Only if you use String or System
options.D: Only for applet programs

mcqs.explanation: java.lang is the only package automatically imported by the Java compiler into every source file. It contains fundamental classes (String, System, Math, Integer, Object) so essential that they're always available. Writing 'import java.lang.*;' is redundant (though harmless).

mcqs.question: To create a package named 'myPackage', what statement goes at the top of the .java file?

options.A: create package myPackage;
options.B: package myPackage;
options.C: namespace myPackage;
options.D: package = myPackage;

mcqs.explanation: 'package myPackage;' is the correct syntax. This statement declares that the class in this file belongs to the 'myPackage' package. The .class file must then be placed in a directory named 'myPackage' relative to the classpath root.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between 'import java.util.Scanner;' and 'import java.util.*;'?

options.A: They are identical
options.B: First imports only Scanner; second imports all public classes in java.util
options.C: First imports all classes; second imports only Scanner
options.D: The wildcard form is slower at runtime

mcqs.explanation: 'import java.util.Scanner;' imports only the Scanner class. 'import java.util.*;' imports all public classes in java.util (Scanner, ArrayList, HashMap, etc.). The wildcard has no runtime performance impact — it only affects compile-time class resolution.

mcqs.question: Can java.util.concurrent be considered a sub-package of java.util?

options.A: No — packages cannot be nested
options.B: Yes — java.util.concurrent is a sub-package of java.util
options.C: Only if java.util.concurrent explicitly imports java.util
options.D: Only if concurrent is declared inside java.util

mcqs.explanation: java.util.concurrent is a sub-package of java.util in terms of naming convention and directory structure. However, in Java, sub-packages are NOT automatically imported with 'import java.util.*;' — you must explicitly import 'import java.util.concurrent.*;' separately.

mcqs.question: What does 'import java.util.*;' NOT do?

options.A: Make ArrayList available without full qualification
options.B: Import java.util.concurrent classes
options.C: Make Scanner available without full qualification
options.D: Make HashMap available

mcqs.explanation: Wildcard imports do NOT import sub-packages. 'import java.util.*;' imports all classes in java.util but does NOT import classes from java.util.concurrent, java.util.function, or any other sub-package. Sub-packages must be imported separately.

mcqs.question: A developer writes 'package com.project.util;' in MyHelper.java but places the file in 'C:\src\MyHelper.java' (not in com/project/util/ directory). What happens when compiling with javac?

options.A: Compilation succeeds; the JVM auto-creates the directory
options.B: Compilation may succeed, but runtime class loading will fail because the class won't be found at the expected path
options.C: Compilation error: file not in correct directory
options.D: The package declaration is ignored

mcqs.explanation: javac typically compiles the file regardless of directory placement (the package statement is in source). However, when running, the JVM looks for com.project.util.MyHelper at 'classpath/com/project/util/MyHelper.class'. If the .class file isn't at that path (or doesn't get placed there with -d), class loading fails at runtime.

mcqs.question: Why is the reverse domain name convention (e.g., com.oracle.java) used for package naming?

options.A: It is required by the Java compiler
options.B: Domain names are globally unique, making package names globally unique and avoiding conflicts between different organizations' packages
options.C: It speeds up class loading
options.D: Internet domains are shorter names

mcqs.explanation: Internet domain names are globally unique (organizations register distinct domains). Reversing the domain (com.oracle → oracle.com) and appending project names creates package names that are globally unique by construction. This prevents package name conflicts when code from different organizations is used together.

mcqs.question: Does 'import' make a copy of the class in the current package?

options.A: Yes — import physically copies the class
options.B: No — import only tells the compiler to look for the class in the specified package; no copying occurs
options.C: Import caches the class for faster loading
options.D: Import downloads the class from the internet

mcqs.explanation: Import statements are purely a compile-time convenience. They tell the compiler what full package path to use when it encounters a short class name. No copying, caching, or downloading occurs. At runtime, the JVM loads class bytecode from the classpath as needed.

mcqs.question: If a class in package 'com.app' needs to use java.util.ArrayList, can it be used WITHOUT any import statement?

options.A: No — import is always required for other-package classes
options.B: Yes — by using the fully qualified name 'java.util.ArrayList' everywhere it is referenced
options.C: Only if java.util is a sub-package of com.app
options.D: Only for JDK built-in classes

mcqs.explanation: Import statements are optional conveniences. You can always use a class without importing by writing its fully qualified name everywhere: 'java.util.ArrayList list = new java.util.ArrayList();'. Imports just allow you to write 'ArrayList' instead of the full path.

mcqs.question: What is the relationship between Java packages and Java modules (introduced in Java 9)?

options.A: Modules replaced packages entirely in Java 9
options.B: Modules group related packages and explicitly declare dependencies between modules; packages remain as organizational units within modules
options.C: Modules and packages are identical
options.D: Modules are packages with at least 100 classes

mcqs.explanation: Java 9's module system (Project Jigsaw) adds a higher-level organizational unit above packages. A module is a group of related packages with an explicit module-info.java that declares which packages it exports and which modules it requires. Packages remain unchanged as the lower-level organizational unit within modules.

mcqs.question: Can a package span multiple .jar files or directories?

options.A: No — a package must be in a single directory or .jar
options.B: Yes — as long as all locations are in the classpath, the JVM finds all classes of the same package across multiple locations
options.C: Only if the package is named 'default'
options.D: Only for java.* packages

mcqs.explanation: A package can be split across multiple .jar files or directories, all present in the classpath. The JVM searches all classpath entries and combines classes from the same package from all locations. This is how the JDK itself is structured — different JDK JARs contribute to the same java.* packages.

mcqs.question: What is a 'package-info.java' file and what is its purpose?

options.A: It lists all class files in a package
options.B: It provides package-level documentation (Javadoc) and can contain package-level annotations
options.C: It is required for compilation of any package
options.D: It stores the package's version number

mcqs.explanation: package-info.java is an optional special file that allows adding Javadoc comments for the entire package (visible in generated documentation) and package-level annotations. It is not required for compilation but is a best practice for well-documented libraries.

mcqs.question: If a developer at oracle.com creates a package 'com.oracle.db' and another developer at oracle.com creates 'com.oracle.network', why is there no naming conflict?

options.A: Oracle owns the com.oracle namespace; different teams can create sub-packages without conflict
options.B: com.oracle is registered as a global trademark
options.C: The JDK automatically prevents naming conflicts
options.D: Package names are case-sensitive, preventing conflicts

mcqs.explanation: Since oracle.com is a unique domain, com.oracle is uniquely theirs. Any sub-package under com.oracle (com.oracle.db, com.oracle.network, etc.) is controlled by Oracle. Different teams within Oracle create different sub-packages under their namespace, avoiding conflicts with other organizations.

mcqs.question: Why do Java packages improve code maintainability?

options.A: Packages automatically fix bugs in the code
options.B: Grouping related classes in packages makes it easier to locate, update, and replace entire functional units; changes within a package are isolated from other packages
options.C: Packages reduce the number of classes needed
options.D: Packages enforce coding standards automatically

mcqs.explanation: Packages improve maintainability through modularity: related classes are grouped, making them easier to find and understand; a package can be updated or replaced without affecting other packages (if its public API is preserved); access control (package-private) hides internal details from the rest of the system.

mcqs.question: A class 'Config' in package 'com.app.internal' has default access. Can 'com.app.Main' use it?

options.A: Yes — com.app.Main and com.app.internal.Config are in the same overall namespace
options.B: No — com.app and com.app.internal are different packages; default access doesn't cross package boundaries
options.C: Only if Main imports com.app.internal
options.D: Yes — parent package classes have access to sub-package classes

mcqs.explanation: In Java, 'com.app' and 'com.app.internal' are two completely separate, independent packages. The hierarchical naming is just a convention — there is no automatic access between parent and child packages. Default-access Config in 'com.app.internal' is not accessible from 'com.app.Main'. Make it public if cross-package access is needed.
